segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of one of the greatest novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving through Charles Dickens' Bleak House — chapter by chapter, passage by passage, character by glorious character.
We begin, as Dickens himself begins, in fog.
Not just the literal fog rolling off the Thames and into the Court of Chancery — but the fog of class, of law, of self-deception that hangs over every character in this novel.
Three extraordinary readers have joined me today, and I want to introduce them properly.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don — a traditionalist critic who has spent a lifetime reading Dickens on Dickens' own terms.
For Edmund, the moral imagination is everything — and he'll remind us, when we're tempted by grand political readings, to look first at the individual soul on the page.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who has spent years inside the actual machinery of Victorian institutions — the courts, the Poor Laws, the whole creaking apparatus.
He'll tell us what Chancery actually was — and why that matters enormously for how we read this novel.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times since.
She'll keep us honest about the experience of the page — what moves, what delights, what stops you in your tracks.
Welcome, all three of you.
Thank you — it is a genuine pleasure to begin here, at the beginning, which Dickens makes so impossibly difficult to abandon.

I want to say something about Sir Leicester Dedlock before we go any further — because he is introduced in Chapter Two with a portrait so devastatingly precise that one almost feels sympathy for the man.
Dickens gives us the measure of him in a single sentence, and I think it deserves to be read aloud.
"He has a general opinion that the world might get on without hills but would be done up without Dedlocks."
That is not satire wielded from a distance — that is surgical.

Dickens understands Sir Leicester completely — his honour, his obstinacy, his perfectly calibrated unreasonableness — and renders him at once ridiculous and, in the strange way of great fiction, rather magnificent.
The fog the novel opens with is not, I would insist, merely a metaphor for institutional corruption.

It is the moral atmosphere in which characters of this precise type — honourable, obstinate, truthful, and perfectly unreasonable — move through their lives absolutely convinced of their own clarity of vision.
Edmund is right that the portrait is surgical — and it becomes even sharper when you understand what Chancery actually was.
Sir Leicester's attitude toward the suit in Jarndyce and Jarndyce is not merely comic — it is historically precise.
Dickens tells us that Sir Leicester regards Chancery as, and I'm reading here,
"a something devised in conjunction with a variety of other somethings by the perfection of human wisdom for the eternal settlement of everything."
That phrase — 'a something' — is doing tremendous work.
Sir Leicester cannot name what Chancery actually does because, at some level, he has never needed to know.
The Court of Chancery in Dickens' day was a jurisdiction of genuinely catastrophic dysfunction — cases lingered for decades, costs consumed entire estates.
And yet there it is — Dickens captures perfectly the ruling-class instinct that even institutional chaos, so long as it is British and constitutional, must not be questioned.
The comparison to Wat Tyler at the end of that passage is not an accident — it is Sir Leicester's private horror: the spectre of popular revolt lurking behind any criticism of the status quo.
What strikes me — and I noticed this on every re-reading — is the sheer audacity of Dickens' comedy in these early chapters.
He gives us Sir Leicester, this perfectly poised monument to class and self-regard, and then he just — stands back and lets the prose do the demolition.

What I love particularly is the way the Chesney Wold description in Chapter Twenty-Eight extends this — it becomes almost pastoral, almost beautiful, before you realise you're being seduced by the same fog the novel is critiquing.
Dickens writes of the ancient house, and listen to this texture,
"where the ivy and the moss have had time to mature, and the gnarled and warted elms and the umbrageous oaks stand deep in the fern and leaves of a hundred years."
That word — 'umbrageous' — is doing so much at once.
It means shadow-giving, shade-heavy — and 'umbrage' of course is also resentment, grievance.
Chesney Wold is beautiful, yes — but it is also shade, and it takes offence, and it does not forgive encroachment.
That, to me, is Dickens at the very height of his powers — where the atmosphere and the argument are identical.
Caroline has put her finger on something I find essential — and which I think is often missed in readings that rush toward indictment.
Dickens genuinely loves what Chesney Wold represents — the weight of tradition, the accumulated dignity of place.
And Sir Leicester, for all his absurdity, is not a villain — he is an honest man trapped inside a false view of the world.
There is a passage — Sir Leicester in my Lady's room, reading from his newspaper with an air of perfect authority — that illustrates this precisely.
"The man who wrote this article," he says, "nodding at the fire as if he were nodding down at the man from a mount — has a well-balanced mind."
That 'nodding down from a mount' — it is the whole man in six words.
He is not cruel, not consciously condescending — he simply inhabits an altitude so long established that he has ceased to notice it.
That, I would argue, is the fog — not an externally imposed corruption, but an internally sustained one.
I don't entirely disagree with Edmund — but I'd put it slightly differently.
The fog — and Dickens is quite deliberate about this — is also structural.
Sir Leicester's comfortable vagueness about what Chancery actually does is not merely a personal failure of curiosity — it is a class position, maintained because investigation would be subversive.
Dickens makes this explicit — and quite savagely — when he notes that any complaint about Chancery would be, in Sir Leicester's private cosmology, an invitation to Wat Tyler.
The not-knowing is not innocent.
It is a form of power — the power to remain above the consequences of the systems you sustain.

And there's a wonderful dramatic irony lurking beneath all of this — because there's another voice in these early chapters who sees Chancery with perfect clarity, and who couldn't be more different from Sir Leicester.
Skimpole — Harold Skimpole — who is also articulate about Chancery's absurdities, but for reasons of the most gorgeous self-serving indolence.
He tells Esther, with sublime effrontery, that Richard's visions of Chancery fortune are simply — poetic.
"In old times the woods and solitudes were made joyous to the shepherd by the imaginary piping and dancing of Pan and the nymphs."
Richard is the 'pastoral Richard,' brightening the dull Inns of Court — and Skimpole finds it all very agreeable.
What's so brilliant and so frightening about this passage is that Skimpole knows perfectly well that the legal abuses are abuses — he simply refuses to be a 'growling fellow' about it.
Sir Leicester doesn't see the fog because he lives in it.
Skimpole sees it perfectly — and finds it charming.
That distinction — blindness versus chosen comfort — feels like the key that unlocks much of what follows in this novel.
And the fog, of course, touches everyone — not just the aristocrats and the aesthetes.
In our next segment, we move deeper into Chancery itself — and into the lives of the people it destroys.

segments.title: Chancery's Victims: Jo and the Law's Cruelty

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked — the podcast that takes Dickens' great legal epic apart, slowly and with relish.
I'm your host, and today we are going deep into the machinery of Chancery — not just as background scenery, but as the engine of cruelty at the novel's heart.
Joining me, as ever, are three remarkable readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, moral critic, and the man most likely to defend the Lord Chancellor on grounds of literary necessity.
Professor James Blackstone — legal historian, specialist in Victorian institutions, and someone who reads the Chancery passages with something close to professional fury.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt — book critic, five-time reader of this novel, and the one among us most likely to make us stop and hear a sentence again.
The question before us today: what does Chancery actually do to people — and how does Dickens make us feel it?
James, you know the historical reality of these courts better than almost anyone. Where shall we begin?
Let's begin with that famous opening chapter — because Dickens doesn't waste a syllable in establishing exactly what Chancery is.
He gives us three figures in that courtroom, and each one is a different stage of the same disease.
The mad old woman with her reticule full of paper matches — that's the end stage.
The prisoner trying to purge himself of contempt — the middle, grinding stage.
And the ruined suitor from Shropshire, still waiting, still watching the judge, voice ready — the early stage, when hope has not quite died.
What's historically precise is how accurately Dickens maps the real procedural traps.
The prisoner in contempt — that was a genuine vice of the system.
You could be held in contempt for failing to comply with an order you lacked the money to comply with — and the court would simply wait for you to die.
What strikes me about that passage — and James is quite right about the accuracy — is the particular quality of Dickens' cruelty toward his own characters.
He gives the ruined suitor from Shropshire no name.
That is the most devastating thing in the passage — not the system's cruelty, but Dickens' decision that this man does not merit a name.
Chancery has already done its work on him before the novel begins.
There is a line I keep returning to — about the Chancellor having made this man's existence desolate.
'Who can by no means be made to understand that the Chancellor is legally ignorant of his existence after making it desolate for a quarter of a century.'
Legally ignorant of his existence — while having destroyed it.
That is not satire. That is something far colder.
And then there's Krook — who is, of course, the novel's most outrageous symbolic joke.
The rag-and-bottle man who mirrors the Lord Chancellor — who hoards everything and disgorges nothing.
What I love is that Dickens lets Krook voice his own metaphor, completely unselfconsciously.
He says it with this wonderful plainness — let me read it:
'There's no great odds betwixt us. We both grub on in a muddle.'
'We both grub on in a muddle.' Eight words — and it contains the whole novel's verdict on the law.
Not evil, not conspiracy — just muddle. Institutional, self-perpetuating, catastrophic muddle.
That word 'muddle' is doing remarkable work, and Caroline is right to press on it.
Because one of the things that made Chancery so devastating — historically — was precisely that no one was clearly to blame.
The solicitors were doing their jobs. The judges were following precedent. The clerks were copying documents.
But then listen to what Krook tells us about Tom Jarndyce — the man who became suicidal, who warned everyone he met.
'It's being ground to bits in a slow mill; it's being roasted at a slow fire; it's being stung to death by single bees; it's being drowned by drops; it's going mad by grains.'
Five metaphors, each one adding a new dimension of slow suffering — and note that every single one of them is slow.
Not violent. Not dramatic. Inexorable.
That is the legal historian's nightmare — and Dickens understood it in his bones.
I want to consider what Kenge says at the end of the novel — because it provides a kind of terrible counterpoint to Tom Jarndyce's litany.
Kenge, that magnificent monument of self-regarding complacency, eulogises the very case that has ruined dozens.
He says — and one must savour this — it was a 'great cause,' a 'protracted cause,' a 'complex cause.'
'Jarndyce and Jarndyce has been termed, not inaptly, a monument of Chancery practice.'
'Not inaptly' — that little hedge is perfect.
The man cannot even allow himself an unqualified statement of pride — and yet the pride is absolute.
Tom Jarndyce said it was going mad by grains. Kenge calls it a monument.
The distance between those two statements is the moral distance Dickens asks us to measure.
And into all of this comes Richard — and that passage in Lincoln's Inn is, for me, one of the most heartbreaking in the novel.
He walks out of Symond's Inn into actual sunshine — Dickens bothers to note there happens to be sunshine there today — and it means nothing.
Because the narrator then gives us that terrible list — those shadows on loungers who came before him.
'The bent head, the bitten nail, the lowering eye, the lingering step, the purposeless and dreamy air, the good consuming and consumed, the life turned sour.'
'The good consuming and consumed' — that chiasmus, that perfect grammatical folding back on itself.
Richard is being both subject and object of his own destruction simultaneously.
And then that final question: 'why should one be different from ten thousand?'
It's the most hopeless sentence in a novel full of hopeless sentences.
That question — 'why should one be different from ten thousand' — is where Dickens most directly addresses the structural logic of the institution.
Chancery did not ruin people by accident. It ruined people by design — or rather, by the accumulated logic of ten thousand precedents.
The novel gives us the case's formal name very early — just that bare announcement from Tulkinghorn:
'In Chancery. Between John Jarndyce—'
That interruption — the dash — is everything.
The case never finishes being read. The case never finishes, full stop.
And Dickens understood — this is what gives the novel its documentary authority — that the real horror was not drama but duration.
Duration — that's exactly the right word, and it haunts the whole novel.
The fog, the mud, the case that never ends — Dickens builds a world in which time itself becomes the instrument of punishment.
We'll return — after the break — to the human cost of that punishment: to Jo, to Richard, and to what it means when a system cannot see its victims.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great fog-bound novel apart — slowly, carefully, and with great affection.
Today we're deep in the wreckage of Richard Carstone — a young man who might have been anything and who, instead, becomes a casualty of Chancery.
With me to work through what Dickens is doing — and why it still matters — are three readers who know this novel in quite different ways.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and lifelong student of the Victorian novel — he reads Richard's ruin as a story about character, not circumstance.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who specialises in Victorian institutions — he knows what Chancery actually did to people, and he is not inclined to be sentimental about it.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times — she brings us back to the experience of reading, sentence by sentence.
Edmund, let's begin with you — because the question of Richard's destruction is, at its heart, a question about moral responsibility.
Is Richard a victim, or is he the author of his own ruin?
That is precisely the question, and I'm afraid the answer is uncomfortable for those who wish to apportion blame entirely elsewhere.
Richard Carstone is not destroyed by Chancery in the way that a man is destroyed by a flood or a fever — by something wholly external to himself.
He is destroyed by a weakness of will that the lawsuit finds out — as a cold wind finds out a thin coat.
Jarndyce sees it with terrible clarity quite early, when he counsels both Richard and Ada in that devastating scene.
The text I have in mind runs — and Dickens gives it to Jarndyce in plain, almost legislative prose —
"I ask you wholly to relinquish, for the present, any tie but your relationship."
It is an act of extraordinary self-denial on Jarndyce's part — he loves these young people — and Richard cannot hear it.
That incapacity to hear good counsel — that is the flaw Dickens is anatomising.
I take the point about character — I do — but I think we need to be precise about what the lawsuit actually was, and what it did to a young man standing at its edge.
The Court of Chancery in the mid-nineteenth century was not simply slow — it was a machine that produced expectation and then withheld resolution, sometimes for generations.
Richard has been told, from childhood, that there is money — his money — somewhere in that system.
Edmund speaks of a weakness of will, and perhaps that is right — but Edmund, I'd ask you: what is will, when it is formed in that kind of atmosphere?

Dickens understood — as I think only someone who had seen a debtor's prison from the inside of a family could — that certain institutions warp the moral imagination before a person ever chooses anything.
I wouldn't dispute that the institution is malign — Dickens makes that abundantly, almost oppressively, clear from the first page.
But there are other young men in the novel formed in equally difficult conditions who do not go under.
Woodcourt comes from nothing — less than nothing — and retains his integrity entire.
Dickens is not writing a case study in institutional determinism.
He is writing a novel about what we choose to believe — and what we choose to believe about ourselves.
What strikes me, reading these chapters again, is how Dickens shows Richard's self-deception becoming perfectly sincere — that's the terrible thing.
Esther notices it, and she can barely bring herself to name it.
There's a passage that chills me every time I read it — Esther is reflecting on what Woodcourt has told her about Richard's state of mind —
"It revived a fear I had had before that my dear girl's little property would be absorbed by Mr. Vholes and that Richard's justification to himself would be sincerely this."
"Sincerely this" — two words, and they carry the full weight of the tragedy.
Richard isn't lying to himself in any simple way — he has genuinely re-arranged the world so that his obsession looks like devotion to Ada.
That is psychologically exact — and it's Dickens at the very top of his powers.
And Vholes is the necessary third party in that arrangement — the legal system's agent, feeding on Richard's expectation with impeccable professional courtesy.
What Dickens understood about Vholes — and what remains completely true of certain legal professionals today — is that the conflict of interest is structural, not personal.
Vholes does not need to wish Richard ill.
The system does the wishing for him.
There's a moment — almost comic, almost heartbreaking — when Woodcourt first visits Richard at Symond's Inn and Richard greets him with this extraordinary line.
He cries out — and I can hear the animation in it even now —
"Woodcourt, my dear fellow, you come upon my vision like a ghost."
He means it as warmth — as delight at seeing an old friend.
But the word he reaches for is "ghost" — and Dickens never reaches for the wrong word.
Richard is already haunted — by the case, by lost time, by the person he was going to be.
That is beautifully observed — and it connects to something I've been turning over since James raised the question of what institutions do to the moral imagination.
Consider what Dickens does with Bucket in the very same novel — a man who also operates entirely within the system, who also plays for high stakes.
The narrator describes him — and this is one of Dickens' great character sketches in brief —

"From the expression of his face he might be a famous whist-player for a large stake — say a hundred guineas certain — with the game in his hand, but with a high reputation involved in his playing his hand out to the last card in a masterly way."
Bucket plays the game — the real game, I mean — and plays it without self-deception, without complaint, and without losing himself.
Richard plays the same system and loses everything — including, finally, himself.
The difference is not in the system.
I'll grant you Bucket — though Bucket has the considerable advantage of being on the right side of the institutional power, not waiting on its verdict.
But I think the whist metaphor is worth dwelling on — because Dickens chooses it very precisely.
Whist is a game of skill and memory — it rewards the player who can hold the whole shape of the game in mind while concealing their own hand.
Richard, by contrast, has been playing — or rather, being played — in a game where the rules shift and the deck is never quite complete.
That is the distinction Dickens is drawing, I think — not between character and institution, but between the man who understands the game and the man who is consumed by it.
What I keep coming back to is Esther's position in all of this — because she is watching it happen and is nearly powerless to stop it.
And she is watching it through the medium of Woodcourt's account — which is itself a kind of double removal from the event.
Dickens layers his narrative with extraordinary care — Woodcourt tells Esther, Esther tells us, and through both of those tellings we feel the reluctance to name what is being named.
There's also this quiet note at the end of the passage — "the shade was still between me and my darling" — referring to Ada.
It is a tiny phrase, but it carries all the estrangement that Richard's obsession has caused — not just to himself, but to the two women who love him most.
What strikes me, listening to all three of you, is that Dickens refuses to let any single explanation settle.
Richard is a victim — and Richard makes choices.
The system is corrupt — and the human capacity for self-deception gives it all the help it needs.
In the next part of today's episode, we'll be turning to the women around Richard — Ada, Esther, the quiet heroism of ordinary love — and asking what Dickens thought devotion was actually worth.

segments.title: Secrets in the Drawing Room: Lady Dedlock's Burden

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great fog-bound novel apart, passage by passage, to see what's really inside.

I'm your host, and today we're deep in the territory this novel does better than almost any other in English fiction — the territory of secrets, of surfaces, of what people show and what they conceal.
Our focus today is Lady Dedlock — one of Dickens' most extraordinary creations — and the slow, terrible pressure that builds around her.
With me today are three people whose company I always find indispensable when the novel gets this dark and this precise.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Bleak House as a novel fundamentally about character — about what people are made of when circumstance closes in.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who knows exactly what these institutions looked like from the inside, and what they did to the people caught inside them.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read this novel five times and still finds new things to marvel at — and to be angry about.
Caroline, I want to start with you, because you've always said the novel announces Lady Dedlock's secret before she has any idea we're watching her.
That opening chapter in Lincolnshire — what is Dickens doing there?
What he's doing is something almost unbearably cunning — and it works on you differently depending on whether it's your first reading or your fifth.
On a first reading, that Lincolnshire chapter feels like pure atmosphere — that extraordinary, sodden, magnificent description of the estate.
But buried at the end of it is a moment that changes everything once you know the story.
Dickens tells us, so quietly, that Lady Dedlock is looking out of her boudoir window at a keeper's lodge.
She sees a child chased by a woman, running out into the rain to meet a man coming through the gate.
And then this — the most devastating bracket in the entire novel:
"My Lady Dedlock, who is childless, looking out in the early twilight from her boudoir at a keeper's lodge...has been put quite out of temper."
That word, childless.
He just puts it there, in parentheses, as if it's merely a biographical fact about an aristocratic woman.
And then he says she was "put out of temper" — this magnificent, composed woman — by the sight of a child running to its father.
On a re-read, you can barely breathe through it.
Caroline is quite right that the bracketed word does enormous work — but I want to dwell on what Dickens is doing with the landscape before we arrive there.
That Lincolnshire passage is, in my view, one of the most accomplished sustained pieces of prose Dickens ever wrote.
Consider the moral weight of the description: the trees soaked through, the deer leaving quagmires where they pass, the rifle shot losing its sharpness in the moist air.
Nothing is clean, nothing is firm, nothing resolves.
And then we are given this:
"The view from my Lady Dedlock's own windows is alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink."
Lead-coloured. Indian ink.
Both colours of something being written down — something being recorded — and both colours of death.
What Dickens understands, and what separates this from mere atmospheric writing, is that the landscape is the condition of her soul — not a symbol of it, the condition of it.
She cannot escape what that view discloses about her, any more than she can escape what Tulkinghorn knows.

I want to come at this from a slightly different angle, if I may — because before we can fully feel the weight of what Dickens is doing with Lady Dedlock, we need to understand what Tulkinghorn actually is.
He is a family solicitor to the Dedlock estate — which in Victorian practice meant something quite specific.
He is the custodian of secrets that legally belong to the family, and yet he holds them — in his own person — as a kind of power.
There was no equivalent in law to a modern concept of professional confidentiality that actually protected the client.
The information was his, in a very real sense.
And Dickens captures this with that devastating little portrait scene — where Tulkinghorn looks at Lady Dedlock's picture and says:
"Who is this? 'Lady Dedlock.' Ha! A very good likeness in its way, but it wants force of character."
He is standing in front of a painting of the woman whose most intimate secret he holds, and he calls her characterless.
That is not cruelty exactly — it's something colder than cruelty.
It is the judgment of a man who has classified her — filed her, one might say — and feels nothing further is required.
And James's point about being filed — classified — connects directly to the scene I find almost unbearable to re-read: the dinner scene in chapter forty-eight.
Tulkinghorn has been to see her. She knows he knows. The whole scene is played in almost total silence.
Dickens tells us she has eaten no dinner — but has twice or thrice poured out water with a steady hand and drunk it.
That steady hand. I come back to it every time.
She is starving and terrified, and she will not let her hand shake.
And Dickens gives us Tulkinghorn's thought — standing there watching her perform this composure — in one sentence:
"This woman thinks Mr. Tulkinghorn, standing on the hearth, again a dark object closing up her view, is a study."
A study. Not a human being in extremis — a study.
And he is described as standing on the hearth — again a dark object closing up her view — which is the most chilling phrase.
He doesn't threaten her. He simply stands between her and whatever she might see beyond him.
That phrase — a dark object closing up her view — deserves more than we usually give it.
Tulkinghorn throughout the novel is described in the language of inanimate things — of stone, of darkness, of obstruction.
He has no inner life that Dickens permits us to see — or rather, Dickens refuses him one, quite deliberately.
What we get instead is that single noun: a study.
Now, one should resist reading Tulkinghorn simply as evil.
He is what his profession made him — a man who has spent forty years reducing persons to cases.
Lady Dedlock is a case. And yet — and this is what gives the chapter its gothic depth — she is clearly not quite a case to him, even now.
She is too composed for that. He cannot quite get purchase on her, and the fascination is unwilling.
Edmund's point about profession is well taken — and it connects to a passage I find almost too funny, given the surrounding darkness.
Dickens spent years reading legal documents — he was a court reporter — and he knew exactly how the legal establishment defended itself against reform.

The Vholes passage — where Mr. Kenge defends the entire corrupt apparatus of Chancery practice by invoking one man's respectability — is essentially a verbatim transcript of every parliamentary committee on legal reform that failed.
The argument was always the same: you cannot reform this institution without destroying a class of worthy men who depend upon it.
Dickens makes Kenge say it with such magnificent self-assurance:
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
As if that were self-evidently a catastrophe.

And then the parliamentary testimony — numbered to question five hundred and seventeen thousand eight hundred and sixty-nine — which proves fatal to the inquiry for ten years, simply by pronouncing Vholes most respectable.
The number is a joke, of course — but it's also not a joke at all.
There were committees. There were questions numbered in the tens of thousands. And nothing changed.
Can I bring us back to Lady Dedlock, though — to the scene that I find most purely moving in everything we've been given today?
It's the moment in chapter thirty-six when Esther is sitting at her favourite spot in the grounds, and she sees someone coming through the wood.
Dickens — through Esther's narration — makes us see the figure reveal itself in stages, at first unrecognisable in the long, leaf-darkened perspective.
And then this:
"By little and little it revealed itself to be a woman's — a lady's — Lady Dedlock's."
Those three dashes. The way the identification narrows — woman, lady, Lady Dedlock — as if Esther is almost afraid to complete the thought.
And then: she was coming with a much quicker step than was usual with her.
The composure has cracked. Lady Dedlock is coming fast, through the wood, towards her daughter.
And neither of them — not yet — knows quite what to do with what they are to each other.
That is a beautiful place to pause — the figure approaching through the leaves, the composure finally breaking.

We've heard today about the landscape as Lady Dedlock's soul, about Tulkinghorn as an object closing up her view, and about institutions so calcified that a single solicitor's good name could freeze reform for a decade.

What strikes me, listening to all three of you, is how completely the private and the institutional are entangled in this novel — how Lady Dedlock's secret and Chancery's secrets are the same kind of secret.
In our next segment, we'll follow the fog further — into the streets, and into the life of Jo, the crossing-sweeper who connects all the worlds this novel holds apart.

segments.title: Narrative Games: How Dickens Tells This Story

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast where we take Dickens' great fog-bound novel apart sentence by sentence — and put it back together with fresh eyes.
Today's segment is about narrative craft — the extraordinary games Dickens plays with how this story is told.
Two voices, two registers, two whole worlds — and Dickens holds them in perfect tension across nearly nine hundred pages.
With me, as always, are Sir Edmund Leigh — Oxford don, moral critic, and the man most likely to quote Burke before breakfast.
Professor James Blackstone, legal historian, who understands the Victorian institutions Dickens is dismantling better than almost anyone alive.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and the reader among us who hears the prose as music — and makes sure we do too.
Edmund, I'd like to start with you — because the passage I've put in your hands is one of the most disarming in the novel.
Esther arrives at Bleak House, and instead of dread or gothic menace, Dickens gives us — warmth.
What is he doing, narratively, in that opening description of the house?
He is doing something quite precise, and I think rather brave.
The name — Bleak House — prepares you for bleakness.
Every gothic convention demands it.
And instead, Esther walks in and finds — quaint engravings, rose-leaves in the drawers, Ada's room all flowers.
The detail is almost comic — surprised birds staring at a trout in a case, as brown and shining as if served with gravy.
But then Dickens lifts the whole passage into something genuinely lyrical.

Listen to how Esther closes the description — with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw.
That rhythm — with its, with its, with its — is pure liturgy.
Dickens is using Esther's voice to create a domestic benediction.
And it matters enormously that it is Esther's voice — because the warmth we feel is inseparable from her character.
The house becomes what she is.
That liturgical quality — yes — I keep coming back to that.
There's something almost prayer-like in the accumulation.
And what I find remarkable is the comedy sitting right alongside it — perfectly at ease.
The four angels of Queen Anne's reign, taking a complacent gentleman to heaven in festoons, with some difficulty.
With some difficulty — that tiny clause does so much work.
It's affectionate mockery — of art, of piety, of the whole slightly absurd business of domestic decoration.
And yet Esther loves it all.
That's the narrative gift of giving her this voice — she can see the absurdity and be wholly moved at the same time.
No other narrator in the novel could do both.
I want to come at this from a slightly different angle, if I may.
Because the name Bleak House carries a very specific legal resonance.
Jarndyce gave it that name in deliberate protest — an act of bitter naming, a private memorial to the damage Chancery had already done to his family.
So when Esther arrives and finds warmth and rose-leaves instead of desolation — that's not Dickens undercutting the gothic.
It's Dickens showing us that Jarndyce has refused the name's logic.
He has willed the house into a counter-reality — through generosity, through care, through sheer force of decency.
The warmth is an argument.
That's a compelling reading, James, and I wouldn't entirely resist it.
Though I'd note that Dickens' other great houses of comfort — the Cheeryble brothers' offices, the Pickwick household — have no such loaded names to overcome.
Dickens understood, as Burke did, that good institutions are not built by programme — they accumulate through habitual generosity.
What Jarndyce has done at Bleak House is essentially conservative — in the finest sense of that word.
He has preserved and furnished and tended — and the result is a home worthy of the name.
Let's turn now to the other narrative register — the omniscient one, which Dickens uses for a very different kind of portraiture.
Edmund, you also have a passage from the Dedlock townhouse — chapter twenty-nine — where the omniscient narrator surveys Sir Leicester amid his pictures.
It's a very different kind of warmth on offer there, isn't it?
Rather magnificently different, yes.
The omniscient narrator can do something Esther is too kind to do — which is to look at Sir Leicester with perfectly calibrated irony.

The house in town wraps his chilled bones in rainbow-coloured wool — that's the narrator's phrase — and Sir Leicester reposes in dignified contentment, honouring the fine arts with a glance of approbation.
Honouring them with a glance.
Not looking, not studying — bestowing a glance.
And then comes the catalogue — which is one of Dickens' most gleefully savage satirical passages.

Three high-backed chairs, a table and cover, long-necked bottle containing wine, one flask, one Spanish female's costume, three-quarter face portrait of Miss Jogg the model, and a suit of armour containing Don Quixote.
The paintings are reduced to auction-room inventories — which is precisely what they deserve.
The omniscient narrator has a sharpness Esther would never permit herself.
The auction catalogue form is doing rather precise cultural work, I think.
These are exactly the kinds of paintings — theatrical costume pieces, orientalist fantasy — that flooded Victorian exhibition rooms and commanded absurd prices.
Dickens knew his readers would recognise the type immediately.
And by listing them as if for a sale, he's pointing to the fundamental transaction — Sir Leicester doesn't experience art, he acquires it.
The collection is a kind of social armour — not unlike Chesney Wold itself.
And yet — and this is what I find so interesting about the omniscient narrator — it's not entirely unkind to Sir Leicester.
There's that image of the house wrapping his chilled bones in rainbow-coloured wool.
It's absurd — but it's also tender.
Dickens consistently reserves the right to feel something for the people he satirises.
Which is precisely why, much later, when Sir Leicester is diminished by illness and betrayal, we find we actually care about him.
The narrator has been preparing us all along.
Caroline puts her finger on something I consider rather important.
By chapter fifty-four, Sir Leicester is a broken man — but he retains a dignity that Dickens will not strip from him.
There is a line in that chapter that I find — quietly devastating.
Sir Leicester Dedlock remains immovable, with the same icy surface upon him, except that he once or twice looks towards Mr. Bucket, as relying on that officer alone of all mankind.
Alone of all mankind.
The great baronet, the embodiment of English aristocratic pride — reduced to trusting a policeman.
And the omniscient narrator renders it without triumph — with something close to compassion.
That dependency is historically rather pointed.
The Metropolitan Police had existed for barely twenty years when Dickens was writing.
For a man of Leicester's class, relying on a detective — and not even a gentleman detective, but a working professional — would have been genuinely shameful.
Dickens is quietly noting that the old arrangements — of honour, of class, of self-sufficient aristocracy — have already failed.
The institutions have let Sir Leicester down — and only a new kind of professional competence can serve him now.
I want to bring in a very small passage — almost a throwaway — that I think speaks directly to how Dickens uses Esther's voice to manage emotional temperature.
It's Esther observing Miss Flite's feeling for Woodcourt — just two lines.
Her gratitude to you, Mr. Woodcourt, is delightful. She is a most affectionate creature, as I have reason to say.
As I have reason to say.
Esther is speaking to Woodcourt — the man she loves — about someone who loves him.
And she cannot quite say what she means — she deflects into an aside, as Esther always does when emotion threatens to overwhelm decorum.
That's the genius of the first-person narration here — the things Esther doesn't say are louder than the things she does.
That observation about suppression is — I think — at the heart of what makes Esther genuinely difficult to read, in the most interesting sense.
There are readers who find her irritating — too modest, too self-effacing, too quick to deny her own perceptions.
And I confess I have some sympathy with the complaint.
But Dickens is making a serious moral point — that genuine goodness does not announce itself.
Esther's indirection is her integrity.

We'll take that thought — Esther's indirection as integrity — into our next segment, where we'll turn to Skimpole and Sir Leicester and the question of what Dickens does with characters who perform their own virtues rather too loudly.
Stay with us.
We've arrived at what I think is the most searching question this novel poses.
Not whether Chancery can be reformed, not whether justice will come — but what hope costs the people who keep faith with it.
We have three passages before us, and they pull in very different directions.
Edmund Leigh has been looking at Jarndyce's vision of those ruined London properties — a piece of writing that is, I think, almost unbearable in its precision.
James Blackstone has been with Gridley — the man from Shropshire — and his magnificent, terrible vow.
And Caroline Woodcourt has been sitting with Jarndyce's great act of selfless advocacy for Esther — the passage where the novel's whole moral argument comes quietly to a head.
Edmund, shall we begin with the ruined street?
Thank you — yes, and I want to begin by insisting on something that can get lost in political readings of this passage.
What Dickens gives us here is not a pamphlet.
It is a prose poem of desolation.
Jarndyce speaks the words, but Dickens has loaded every syllable with Gothic weight.
Listen to the accumulation here — the way each detail compounds the last.

"It is a street of perishing blind houses, with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their hinges and falling asunder, the iron rails peeling away in flakes of rust, the chimneys sinking in, the stone steps to every door (and every door might be death's door) turning stagnant green."
Every door might be death's door.
That parenthesis is not a flourish — it is the entire argument, placed in the very middle of a sentence about material decay.
Edmund is absolutely right about the Gothic register — but I want to add what's underneath it, historically speaking.
These houses are not a fictional invention.
There were real properties in London — real streets — suspended in Chancery for decades, physically deteriorating while lawyers argued over who might eventually own them.
Dickens knew this because he had reported on Chancery proceedings as a young journalist.
And Jarndyce's phrase — "the property of costs" — is not a metaphor.
It was the literal legal reality: the costs had devoured the estate.
And then he closes — and this is the line that stops me every time: "These are the Great Seal's impressions, my dear, all over England — the children know them."
The children know them.
That line has always seemed to me the most quietly devastating in the passage.
The children know them — not the lawyers, not the judges, not the Members of Parliament who might reform the system.
The children.
They have grown up inside the ruin.
It is the normality of catastrophe — and that, I think, is Dickens at his most morally serious.
And now Gridley — who refuses, absolutely refuses, to accept that normality.
James, this is one of the great defiant speeches in all of Victorian fiction, isn't it?
It is — and what makes it great is that Dickens doesn't romanticise Gridley's rage.
Gridley himself admits he is violent.
He has been imprisoned for contempt of court, for threatening his solicitor.
He knows full well that his fury has made his position worse — and he cannot stop.
That tension — between the knowledge that rage is self-destructive and the absolute moral necessity of it — that is what gives this speech its tragic power.
And then comes the vow itself.

"I'll shame them. To the last, I'll show myself in that court to its shame. If I knew when I was going to die, and could be carried there, and had a voice to speak with, I would die there, saying, 'You have brought me here and sent me from here many and many a time. Now send me out feet foremost!'"
Now send me out feet foremost.
That is a man who will not let the institution outlast his witness against it.
What strikes me about Gridley — coming to it again just now — is the phrase "I was a good-enough-tempered man once, I believe."
That "I believe" is heartbreaking.
He is so far from that former self that he can only refer to it as hearsay.
Other people in his county remember him as he was.
He no longer recognises himself.
Chancery has not merely taken his money and his time.
It has taken his self.
That is precisely observed.
And it connects, I think, to something central in Dickens' moral vision — that institutions do not merely fail people.
They corrupt them.
They work upon character — they diminish it, distort it, hollow it out.
Richard Carstone is the novel's most sustained demonstration of this — but Gridley is its most vivid flash of it.
A man consumed — but not quite extinguished.
Which brings us, finally, to the very different kind of hope that Caroline has been tending — Jarndyce's quiet intervention on Esther's behalf.
Because if Gridley is hope exhausted into defiance, this passage is hope — against considerable odds — fulfilled.
This is the passage I find it hardest to read aloud without my voice catching.
Jarndyce has renounced his own claim on Esther — entirely, selflessly — and here we see how far he went in her service.
He sought out Mrs. Woodcourt — that formidable, snobbish woman with all her talk of pedigree and Welsh ancestry — and he confronted her directly.
And the speech he gives her is really a kind of challenge — a moral challenge, delivered with perfect composure.

"'Now, madam,' said I, 'come you, knowing this, and live with us. Come you, and see my child from hour to hour; set what you see against her pedigree, which is this, and this' — for I scorned to mince it — 'and tell me what is the true legitimacy when you shall have quite made up your mind on that subject.'"
"I scorned to mince it."
That is Jarndyce at his most magnificent — not sentimental, not apologetic, but absolutely direct.
He refuses to minimise Esther's illegitimacy, because the whole force of his argument depends on confronting it.
The legal resonance of "legitimacy" in this speech is worth pausing over.
In 1852, the stigma of illegitimacy was not merely social — it carried real legal disabilities.
A child born outside marriage could not inherit, could not hold certain offices, was excluded from legal standing in ways that would shadow a whole life.
Jarndyce's question — "what is the true legitimacy?" — is not merely rhetorical.
It is a direct challenge to the law's definition of a person's worth.
I want to resist, very gently, any reading that turns Jarndyce here into a radical.
He is not arguing against legitimacy as a concept — he is arguing for Esther as an exception.
The moral appeal is particular, not universal.
And I think that is entirely consistent with Dickens' own instincts — which are deeply, almost stubbornly, personal.
Change comes through individual hearts changing — not through systems reforming themselves.
And what makes this passage so moving to me — on every re-reading — is that it comes at the very end, when the reader is already exhausted by everything the novel has put us through.
Richard is dead.
Gridley is dead.
Jo is dead.
And yet here is Jarndyce, speaking with — I can only call it "exultation" — about Esther's future.
Dickens earns this.
He has not spared us anything — and so when the tenderness comes, it is real.
Three passages, and three different answers to the question of what hope looks like at the end of endurance.
Jarndyce's street of blind houses: hope as evidence of what has already been destroyed.
Gridley's deathbed vow: hope transmuted into refusal — into a defiance that survives even the body.
And Jarndyce's act of selfless advocacy: hope as something quietly, stubbornly, tenderly fulfilled.
Edmund Leigh, James Blackstone, Caroline Woodcourt — thank you.
This has been Bleak House Unpacked.
We'll be back with the next episode — until then, read slowly, and read well.

c2:p4.text:
Sir Leicester Dedlock is only a baronet, but there is no mightier
baronet than he. His family is as old as the hills, and infinitely
more respectable. He has a general opinion that the world might get
on without hills but would be done up without Dedlocks. He would on
the whole admit nature to be a good idea (a little low, perhaps, when
not enclosed with a park-fence), but an idea dependent for its
execution on your great county families. He is a gentleman of strict
conscience, disdainful of all littleness and meanness and ready on
the shortest notice to die any death you may please to mention rather
than give occasion for the least impeachment of his integrity. He is
an honourable, obstinate, truthful, high-spirited, intensely
prejudiced, perfectly unreasonable man.
c2:p4.summary: Sir Leicester Dedlock is a baronet of ancient family, rigid principles, and class-bound prejudices who views the social order as naturally ordained with his family at its apex.
c2:p4.best_quote: He has a general opinion that the world might get on without hills but would be done up without Dedlocks

c2:p19.text:
Sir Leicester has no objection to an interminable Chancery suit. It
is a slow, expensive, British, constitutional kind of thing. To be
sure, he has not a vital interest in the suit in question, her part
in which was the only property my Lady brought him; and he has a
shadowy impression that for his name—the name of Dedlock—to be in a
cause, and not in the title of that cause, is a most ridiculous
accident. But he regards the Court of Chancery, even if it should
involve an occasional delay of justice and a trifling amount of
confusion, as a something devised in conjunction with a variety of
other somethings by the perfection of human wisdom for the eternal
settlement (humanly speaking) of everything. And he is upon the whole
of a fixed opinion that to give the sanction of his countenance to
any complaints respecting it would be to encourage some person in the
lower classes to rise up somewhere—like Wat Tyler.
c2:p19.summary: Sir Leicester accepts the Chancery suit's interminable nature as a properly British institution, regarding even its inefficiency as part of the constitutional order; his main concern is that his name be prominent in the title.
c2:p19.best_quote: he has a shadowy impression that for his name—the name of Dedlock—to be in a cause, and not in the title of that cause, is a most ridiculous accident

c28:p37.text:
Sir Leicester is content enough that the ironmaster should feel that
there is no hurry there; there, in that ancient house, rooted in that
quiet park, where the ivy and the moss have had time to mature, and
the gnarled and warted elms and the umbrageous oaks stand deep in the
fern and leaves of a hundred years; and where the sun-dial on the
terrace has dumbly recorded for centuries that time which was as much
the property of every Dedlock—while he lasted—as the house and
lands. Sir Leicester sits down in an easy-chair, opposing his repose
and that of Chesney Wold to the restless flights of ironmasters.
c28:p37.summary: Sir Leicester finds comfort in Chesney Wold's timelessness and repose, opposing it to the restless commercial flights of modern ironmasters.
c28:p37.best_quote: where the ivy and the moss have had time to mature, and the gnarled and warted elms and the umbrageous oaks stand deep in the fern and leaves of a hundred years

c29:p3.text:
Sir Leicester sits in my Lady’s room—that room in which Mr.
Tulkinghorn read the affidavit in Jarndyce and Jarndyce—particularly
complacent. My Lady, as on that day, sits before the fire with her
screen in her hand. Sir Leicester is particularly complacent because
he has found in his newspaper some congenial remarks bearing directly
on the floodgates and the framework of society. They apply so happily
to the late case that Sir Leicester has come from the library to my
Lady’s room expressly to read them aloud. “The man who wrote this
article,” he observes by way of preface, nodding at the fire as if he
were nodding down at the man from a mount, “has a well-balanced
mind.”
c29:p3.summary: Sir Leicester reads aloud from a newspaper article to Lady Dedlock about social matters, praising the author's balanced mind.

c37:p43.text:
“My dear Miss Summerson, here is our friend Richard,” said Mr.
Skimpole, “full of the brightest visions of the future, which he
evokes out of the darkness of Chancery. Now that’s delightful, that’s
inspiriting, that’s full of poetry! In old times the woods and
solitudes were made joyous to the shepherd by the imaginary piping
and dancing of Pan and the nymphs. This present shepherd, our
pastoral Richard, brightens the dull Inns of Court by making Fortune
and her train sport through them to the melodious notes of a judgment
from the bench. That’s very pleasant, you know! Some ill-conditioned
growling fellow may say to me, ‘What’s the use of these legal and
equitable abuses? How do you defend them?’ I reply, ‘My growling
friend, I DON’T defend them, but they are very agreeable to me. There
is a shepherd—youth, a friend of mine, who transmutes them into
something highly fascinating to my simplicity. I don’t say it is for
this that they exist—for I am a child among you worldly grumblers,
and not called upon to account to you or myself for anything—but it
may be so.’”
c37:p43.summary: Richard asks Esther to arrange a private morning walk so he can justify himself and his relationship with John Jarndyce.

c1:p6.text:
Who happen to be in the Lord Chancellor’s court this murky afternoon
besides the Lord Chancellor, the counsel in the cause, two or three
counsel who are never in any cause, and the well of solicitors before
mentioned? There is the registrar below the judge, in wig and gown;
and there are two or three maces, or petty-bags, or privy purses, or
whatever they may be, in legal court suits. These are all yawning,
for no crumb of amusement ever falls from Jarndyce and Jarndyce (the
cause in hand), which was squeezed dry years upon years ago. The
short-hand writers, the reporters of the court, and the reporters of
the newspapers invariably decamp with the rest of the regulars when
Jarndyce and Jarndyce comes on. Their places are a blank. Standing on
a seat at the side of the hall, the better to peer into the curtained
sanctuary, is a little mad old woman in a squeezed bonnet who is
always in court, from its sitting to its rising, and always expecting
some incomprehensible judgment to be given in her favour. Some say
she really is, or was, a party to a suit, but no one knows for
certain because no one cares. She carries some small litter in a
reticule which she calls her documents, principally consisting of
paper matches and dry lavender. A sallow prisoner has come up, in
custody, for the half-dozenth time to make a personal application “to
purge himself of his contempt,” which, being a solitary surviving
executor who has fallen into a state of conglomeration about accounts
of which it is not pretended that he had ever any knowledge, he is
not at all likely ever to do. In the meantime his prospects in life
are ended. Another ruined suitor, who periodically appears from
Shropshire and breaks out into efforts to address the Chancellor at
the close of the day’s business and who can by no means be made to
understand that the Chancellor is legally ignorant of his existence
after making it desolate for a quarter of a century, plants himself
in a good place and keeps an eye on the judge, ready to call out “My
Lord!” in a voice of sonorous complaint on the instant of his rising.
A few lawyers’ clerks and others who know this suitor by sight linger
on the chance of his furnishing some fun and enlivening the dismal
weather a little.
c1:p6.summary: The court contains a miscellany of tragic figures: a mad woman with paper-match 'documents,' a prisoner repeatedly attempting to clear contempt charges, and a ruined suitor from Shropshire who periodically appears to plead to an indifferent Chancellor.

c5:p42.text:
“You see, I have so many things here,” he resumed, holding up the
lantern, “of so many kinds, and all as the neighbours think (but THEY
know nothing), wasting away and going to rack and ruin, that that’s
why they have given me and my place a christening. And I have so many
old parchmentses and papers in my stock. And I have a liking for rust
and must and cobwebs. And all’s fish that comes to my net. And I
can’t abear to part with anything I once lay hold of (or so my
neighbours think, but what do THEY know?) or to alter anything, or to
have any sweeping, nor scouring, nor cleaning, nor repairing going on
about me. That’s the way I’ve got the ill name of Chancery. I don’t
mind. I go to see my noble and learned brother pretty well every day,
when he sits in the Inn. He don’t notice me, but I notice him.
There’s no great odds betwixt us. We both grub on in a muddle. Hi,
Lady Jane!”
c5:p42.summary: Krook explains his hoarding habits, his affection for old papers and parchments, his refusal to clean or part with anything, and his identification with the real Lord Chancellor. He introduces his cat, Lady Jane.
c5:p42.best_quote: We both grub on in a muddle.

c5:p56.text:
“Aye!” said the old man, coming slowly out of his abstraction. “Yes!
Tom Jarndyce—you’ll excuse me, being related; but he was never known
about court by any other name, and was as well known there as—she is
now,” nodding slightly at his lodger. “Tom Jarndyce was often in
here. He got into a restless habit of strolling about when the cause
was on, or expected, talking to the little shopkeepers and telling
’em to keep out of Chancery, whatever they did. ‘For,’ says he, ‘it’s
being ground to bits in a slow mill; it’s being roasted at a slow
fire; it’s being stung to death by single bees; it’s being drowned by
drops; it’s going mad by grains.’ He was as near making away with
himself, just where the young lady stands, as near could be.”
c5:p56.summary: Krook relates the tragic story of Tom Jarndyce, the original plaintiff in the suit, who repeatedly warned others to avoid Chancery's destruction. Tom became suicidal and eventually shot himself at a tavern near Chancery Lane.
c5:p56.best_quote: For, says he, it's being ground to bits in a slow mill; it's being roasted at a slow fire; it's being stung to death by single bees; it's being drowned by drops; it's going mad by grains.

c65:p19.text:
“You are to reflect, Mr. Woodcourt,” observed Mr. Kenge, using his
silver trowel persuasively and smoothingly, “that this has been a
great cause, that this has been a protracted cause, that this has
been a complex cause. Jarndyce and Jarndyce has been termed, not
inaptly, a monument of Chancery practice.”
c65:p19.summary: Mr. Kenge elaborates on the case as a great, complex, and protracted cause demonstrating Chancery practice.

c39:p43.text:
Richard, emerging from the heavy shade of Symond’s Inn into the
sunshine of Chancery Lane—for there happens to be sunshine there
to-day—walks thoughtfully on, and turns into Lincoln’s Inn, and
passes under the shadow of the Lincoln’s Inn trees. On many such
loungers have the speckled shadows of those trees often fallen; on
the like bent head, the bitten nail, the lowering eye, the lingering
step, the purposeless and dreamy air, the good consuming and
consumed, the life turned sour. This lounger is not shabby yet, but
that may come. Chancery, which knows no wisdom but in precedent, is
very rich in such precedents; and why should one be different from
ten thousand?
c39:p43.summary: Richard emerges into sunshine and walks through Lincoln's Inn, but the narrator reflects on how the space has witnessed the deterioration of many Chancery suitors before him, suggesting he may follow the same path.
c39:p43.best_quote: On many such loungers have the speckled shadows of those trees often fallen; on the like bent head, the bitten nail, the lowering eye, the lingering step, the purposeless and dreamy air, the good consuming and consumed, the life turned sour.

c2:p23.summary: Tulkinghorn begins reading the formal preamble of the Chancery case: 'In Chancery. Between John Jarndyce—'

c24:p20.text:
“Ada, my dear,” said Mr. Jarndyce, recovering his cheerfulness,
“these are strong words of advice, but I live in Bleak House and have
seen a sight here. Enough of that. All Richard had to start him in
the race of life is ventured. I recommend to him and you, for his
sake and your own, that he should depart from us with the
understanding that there is no sort of contract between you. I must
go further. I will be plain with you both. You were to confide freely
in me, and I will confide freely in you. I ask you wholly to
relinquish, for the present, any tie but your relationship.”
c24:p20.summary: Jarndyce proposes that Ada and Richard dissolve their romantic engagement and remain only cousins, citing his experience at Bleak House as justification.
c24:p20.best_quote: I ask you wholly to relinquish, for the present, any tie but your relationship.

c51:p37.text:
Afterwards, when Mr. Woodcourt came to reflect on what had passed, he
was so very much impressed by the strength of Richard’s anxiety on
this point that in telling me generally of his first visit to
Symond’s Inn he particularly dwelt upon it. It revived a fear I had
had before that my dear girl’s little property would be absorbed by
Mr. Vholes and that Richard’s justification to himself would be
sincerely this. It was just as I began to take care of Caddy that the
interview took place, and I now return to the time when Caddy had
recovered and the shade was still between me and my darling.

c51:p37.best_quote: It revived a fear I had had before that my dear girl's little property would be absorbed by Mr. Vholes and that Richard's justification to himself would be sincerely this.

c51:p21.text:
“Woodcourt, my dear fellow,” cried Richard, starting up with extended
hands, “you come upon my vision like a ghost.”
c51:p21.summary: Richard enthusiastically welcomes Woodcourt, comparing his sudden appearance to a ghostly visitation.
c51:p21.best_quote: you come upon my vision like a ghost

c54:p1.text:
Thoughtful Mr. Bucket is, as a man may be with weighty work to do,
but composed, sure, confident. From the expression of his face he
might be a famous whist-player for a large stake—say a hundred
guineas certain—with the game in his hand, but with a high
reputation involved in his playing his hand out to the last card in a
masterly way. Not in the least anxious or disturbed is Mr. Bucket
when Sir Leicester appears, but he eyes the baronet aside as he comes
slowly to his easy-chair with that observant gravity of yesterday in
which there might have been yesterday, but for the audacity of the
idea, a touch of compassion.
c54:p1.summary: Bucket is thoughtful but composed, like a skilled gambler with everything at stake, regarding Sir Leicester with observant gravity and possible compassion.
c54:p1.best_quote: From the expression of his face he might be a famous whist-player for a large stake—say a hundred guineas certain—with the game in his hand, but with a high reputation involved in his playing his hand out to the last card in a masterly way.

c2:p2.text:
My Lady Dedlock has returned to her house in town for a few days
previous to her departure for Paris, where her ladyship intends to
stay some weeks, after which her movements are uncertain. The
fashionable intelligence says so for the comfort of the Parisians,
and it knows all fashionable things. To know things otherwise were to
be unfashionable. My Lady Dedlock has been down at what she calls, in
familiar conversation, her “place” in Lincolnshire. The waters are
out in Lincolnshire. An arch of the bridge in the park has been
sapped and sopped away. The adjacent low-lying ground for half a mile
in breadth is a stagnant river with melancholy trees for islands in
it and a surface punctured all over, all day long, with falling rain.
My Lady Dedlock’s place has been extremely dreary. The weather for
many a day and night has been so wet that the trees seem wet through,
and the soft loppings and prunings of the woodman’s axe can make no
crash or crackle as they fall. The deer, looking soaked, leave
quagmires where they pass. The shot of a rifle loses its sharpness in
the moist air, and its smoke moves in a tardy little cloud towards
the green rise, coppice-topped, that makes a background for the
falling rain. The view from my Lady Dedlock’s own windows is
alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink. The vases
on the stone terrace in the foreground catch the rain all day; and
the heavy drops fall—drip, drip, drip—upon the broad flagged
pavement, called from old time the Ghost’s Walk, all night. On
Sundays the little church in the park is mouldy; the oaken pulpit
breaks out into a cold sweat; and there is a general smell and taste
as of the ancient Dedlocks in their graves. My Lady Dedlock (who is
childless), looking out in the early twilight from her boudoir at a
keeper’s lodge and seeing the light of a fire upon the latticed
panes, and smoke rising from the chimney, and a child, chased by a
woman, running out into the rain to meet the shining figure of a
wrapped-up man coming through the gate, has been put quite out of
temper. My Lady Dedlock says she has been “bored to death.”
c2:p2.summary: Lady Dedlock returns to her Lincolnshire estate before departing for Paris, where the landscape is depicted as relentlessly dreary and sodden; her observation of a family scene at a keeper's lodge disrupts her usual composure.
c2:p2.best_quote: The view from my Lady Dedlock's own windows is alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink

c39:p87.text:
“A virtue in which few Englishmen are deficient,” observes Mr.
Tulkinghorn. He has been standing on the hearthstone with his back to
the smoked chimney-piece, and now turns round with his glasses to his
eyes. “Who is this? ‘Lady Dedlock.’ Ha! A very good likeness in its
way, but it wants force of character. Good day to you, gentlemen;
good day!”
c39:p87.summary: Tulkinghorn examines Lady Dedlock's portrait, comments cryptically on its weakness of character, and then takes his leave with a polite farewell.
c39:p87.best_quote: Who is this? 'Lady Dedlock.' Ha! A very good likeness in its way, but it wants force of character.

c48:p105.text:
For a little while they are silent. Lady Dedlock has eaten no dinner,
but has twice or thrice poured out water with a steady hand and drunk
it. She rises from table, takes a lounging-chair, and reclines in it,
shading her face. There is nothing in her manner to express weakness
or excite compassion. It is thoughtful, gloomy, concentrated. “This
woman,” thinks Mr. Tulkinghorn, standing on the hearth, again a dark
object closing up her view, “is a study.”
c48:p105.summary: In the silence that follows, Lady Dedlock maintains thoughtful composure while remaining emotionally turbulent; Tulkinghorn regards her as a fascinating psychological study.
c48:p105.best_quote: This woman,' thinks Mr. Tulkinghorn, standing on the hearth, again a dark object closing up her view, 'is a study.'

c39:p4.text:
But not perceiving this quite plainly—only seeing it by halves in a
confused way—the laity sometimes suffer in peace and pocket, with a
bad grace, and DO grumble very much. Then this respectability of Mr.
Vholes is brought into powerful play against them. “Repeal this
statute, my good sir?” says Mr. Kenge to a smarting client. “Repeal
it, my dear sir? Never, with my consent. Alter this law, sir, and
what will be the effect of your rash proceeding on a class of
practitioners very worthily represented, allow me to say to you, by
the opposite attorney in the case, Mr. Vholes? Sir, that class of
practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth. Now you
cannot afford—I will say, the social system cannot afford—to lose
an order of men like Mr. Vholes. Diligent, persevering, steady, acute
in business. My dear sir, I understand your present feelings against
the existing state of things, which I grant to be a little hard in
your case; but I can never raise my voice for the demolition of a
class of men like Mr. Vholes.” The respectability of Mr. Vholes has
even been cited with crushing effect before Parliamentary committees,
as in the following blue minutes of a distinguished attorney’s
evidence. “Question (number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight
hundred and sixty-nine): If I understand you, these forms of practice
indisputably occasion delay? Answer: Yes, some delay. Question: And
great expense? Answer: Most assuredly they cannot be gone through for
nothing. Question: And unspeakable vexation? Answer: I am not
prepared to say that. They have never given ME any vexation; quite
the contrary. Question: But you think that their abolition would
damage a class of practitioners? Answer: I have no doubt of it.
Question: Can you instance any type of that class? Answer: Yes. I
would unhesitatingly mention Mr. Vholes. He would be ruined.
Question: Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a respectable
man? Answer:”—which proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years—“Mr.
Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man.”
c39:p4.summary: Mr. Kenge's rhetorical defense of legal practitioners like Vholes is presented, along with a mock parliamentary inquiry that demonstrates how institutional self-interest defeats reform through the invocation of Vholes's respectable reputation.
c39:p4.best_quote: Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth.

c36:p18.text:
I was resting at my favourite point after a long ramble, and Charley
was gathering violets at a little distance from me. I had been
looking at the Ghost’s Walk lying in a deep shade of masonry afar off
and picturing to myself the female shape that was said to haunt it
when I became aware of a figure approaching through the wood. The
perspective was so long and so darkened by leaves, and the shadows of
the branches on the ground made it so much more intricate to the eye,
that at first I could not discern what figure it was. By little and
little it revealed itself to be a woman’s—a lady’s—Lady Dedlock’s.
She was alone and coming to where I sat with a much quicker step, I
observed to my surprise, than was usual with her.
c36:p18.summary: As Esther rests at her favorite spot, a woman emerges through the wood—Lady Dedlock, approaching with unusual haste and emotion.

c6:p46.text:
The furniture, old-fashioned rather than old, like the house, was as
pleasantly irregular. Ada’s sleeping-room was all flowers—in chintz
and paper, in velvet, in needlework, in the brocade of two stiff
courtly chairs which stood, each attended by a little page of a stool
for greater state, on either side of the fire-place. Our sitting-room
was green and had framed and glazed upon the walls numbers of
surprising and surprised birds, staring out of pictures at a real
trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with
gravy; at the death of Captain Cook; and at the whole process of
preparing tea in China, as depicted by Chinese artists. In my room
there were oval engravings of the months—ladies haymaking in short
waists and large hats tied under the chin, for June; smooth-legged
noblemen pointing with cocked-hats to village steeples, for October.
Half-length portraits in crayons abounded all through the house, but
were so dispersed that I found the brother of a youthful officer of
mine in the china-closet and the grey old age of my pretty young
bride, with a flower in her bodice, in the breakfast-room. As
substitutes, I had four angels, of Queen Anne’s reign, taking a
complacent gentleman to heaven, in festoons, with some difficulty;
and a composition in needlework representing fruit, a kettle, and an
alphabet. All the movables, from the wardrobes to the chairs and
tables, hangings, glasses, even to the pincushions and scent-bottles
on the dressing-tables, displayed the same quaint variety. They
agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the
whitest linen, and their storing-up, wheresoever the existence of a
drawer, small or large, rendered it possible, of quantities of
rose-leaves and sweet lavender. Such, with its illuminated windows,
softened here and there by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the
starlight night; with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its
hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with
the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and
just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything
we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House.
c6:p46.summary: Detailed description of Bleak House's furnishings in each room, establishing a warm, hospitable environment filled with quirky collections and careful comfort.
c6:p46.best_quote: with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House

c29:p1.text:
But the house in town, which is rarely in the same mind as Chesney
Wold at the same time, seldom rejoicing when it rejoices or mourning
when it mourns, excepting when a Dedlock dies—the house in town
shines out awakened. As warm and bright as so much state may be, as
delicately redolent of pleasant scents that bear no trace of winter
as hothouse flowers can make it, soft and hushed so that the ticking
of the clocks and the crisp burning of the fires alone disturb the
stillness in the rooms, it seems to wrap those chilled bones of Sir
Leicester’s in rainbow-coloured wool. And Sir Leicester is glad to
repose in dignified contentment before the great fire in the library,
condescendingly perusing the backs of his books or honouring the fine
arts with a glance of approbation. For he has his pictures, ancient
and modern. Some of the Fancy Ball School in which art occasionally
condescends to become a master, which would be best catalogued like
the miscellaneous articles in a sale. As “Three high-backed chairs, a
table and cover, long-necked bottle (containing wine), one flask, one
Spanish female’s costume, three-quarter face portrait of Miss Jogg
the model, and a suit of armour containing Don Quixote.” Or “One
stone terrace (cracked), one gondola in distance, one Venetian
senator’s dress complete, richly embroidered white satin costume with
profile portrait of Miss Jogg the model, one Scimitar superbly
mounted in gold with jewelled handle, elaborate Moorish dress (very
rare), and Othello.”
c29:p1.summary: The Dedlock townhouse is warm and bright, where Sir Leicester rests contentedly, examining his collection of art that Dickens satirizes as kitsch.

c54:p79.text:
While this exordium is in hand—and it takes some time—Mr. Bucket,
who has seen through the transparency of Mrs. Snagsby’s vinegar at a
glance, confers with his familiar demon and bestows his shrewd
attention on the Chadbands and Mr. Smallweed. Sir Leicester Dedlock
remains immovable, with the same icy surface upon him, except that he
once or twice looks towards Mr. Bucket, as relying on that officer
alone of all mankind.
c54:p79.summary: Bucket dismisses Mrs. Snagsby's testimony while the others sit listening, and Sir Leicester shows his dependence on Bucket.
c54:p79.best_quote: Sir Leicester Dedlock remains immovable, with the same icy surface upon him, except that he once or twice looks towards Mr. Bucket, as relying on that officer alone of all mankind.

c45:p72.text:
“Her gratitude to you, Mr. Woodcourt, is delightful. She is a most
affectionate creature, as I have reason to say.”
c45:p72.summary: Esther remarks on Miss Flite's affection and gratitude toward Woodcourt.

c43:p80.text:
“It has given me pain, Mr. Jarndyce,” Sir Leicester weightily
proceeded. “I assure you, sir, it has given—me—pain—to learn from
the housekeeper at Chesney Wold that a gentleman who was in your
company in that part of the county, and who would appear to possess a
cultivated taste for the fine arts, was likewise deterred by some
such cause from examining the family pictures with that leisure, that
attention, that care, which he might have desired to bestow upon them
and which some of them might possibly have repaid.” Here he produced
a card and read, with much gravity and a little trouble, through his
eye-glass, “Mr. Hirrold—Herald—Harold—Skampling—Skumpling—I beg
your pardon—Skimpole.”
c43:p80.summary: Sir Leicester reports that Skimpole, when visiting Lincolnshire, was also deterred from viewing Chesney Wold's pictures, which gave him pain to learn.
c43:p80.best_quote: I assure you, sir, it has given—me—pain—to learn from the housekeeper at Chesney Wold that a gentleman who was in your company in that part of the county, and who would appear to possess a cultivated taste for the fine arts, was likewise deterred by some such cause from examining the family pictures with that leisure, that attention, that care, which he might have desired to bestow upon them.

c8:p24.text:
“Bleak House; true. There is, in that city of London there, some
property of ours which is much at this day what Bleak House was then;
I say property of ours, meaning of the suit’s, but I ought to call it
the property of costs, for costs is the only power on earth that will
ever get anything out of it now or will ever know it for anything but
an eyesore and a heartsore. It is a street of perishing blind houses,
with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much
as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their
hinges and falling asunder, the iron rails peeling away in flakes of
rust, the chimneys sinking in, the stone steps to every door (and
every door might be death’s door) turning stagnant green, the very
crutches on which the ruins are propped decaying. Although Bleak
House was not in Chancery, its master was, and it was stamped with
the same seal. These are the Great Seal’s impressions, my dear, all
over England—the children know them!”
c8:p24.summary: Jarndyce describes a street of property nominally belonging to the Jarndyce suit but effectively owned by costs; the houses are in terrible decay, windowless, rusted, and desolate, bearing the Great Seal's mark of Chancery throughout England.

c15:p113.text:
“I have done!” he said, sitting down and wiping his face. “Mr.
Jarndyce, I have done! I am violent, I know. I ought to know it. I
have been in prison for contempt of court. I have been in prison for
threatening the solicitor. I have been in this trouble, and that
trouble, and shall be again. I am the man from Shropshire, and I
sometimes go beyond amusing them, though they have found it amusing,
too, to see me committed into custody and brought up in custody and
all that. It would be better for me, they tell me, if I restrained
myself. I tell them that if I did restrain myself I should become
imbecile. I was a good-enough-tempered man once, I believe. People in
my part of the country say they remember me so, but now I must have
this vent under my sense of injury or nothing could hold my wits
together. It would be far better for you, Mr. Gridley,’ the Lord
Chancellor told me last week, ‘not to waste your time here, and to
stay, usefully employed, down in Shropshire.’ ‘My Lord, my Lord, I
know it would,’ said I to him, ‘and it would have been far better for
me never to have heard the name of your high office, but unhappily
for me, I can’t undo the past, and the past drives me here!’
Besides,” he added, breaking fiercely out, “I’ll shame them. To the
last, I’ll show myself in that court to its shame. If I knew when I
was going to die, and could be carried there, and had a voice to
speak with, I would die there, saying, ‘You have brought me here and
sent me from here many and many a time. Now send me out feet
foremost!’”
c15:p113.summary: Gridley declares he will shame Chancery to the end, vowing that even on his deathbed he would speak his accusation in the courtroom.
c15:p113.best_quote: I'll shame them. To the last, I'll show myself in that court to its shame. If I knew when I was going to die, and could be carried there, and had a voice to speak with, I would die there, saying, 'You have brought me here and sent me from here many and many a time. Now send me out feet foremost!'

c64:p35.text:
“Hush, little woman! Don’t cry; this is to be a day of joy. I have
looked forward to it,” he said exultingly, “for months on months! A
few words more, Dame Trot, and I have said my say. Determined not to
throw away one atom of my Esther’s worth, I took Mrs. Woodcourt into
a separate confidence. ‘Now, madam,’ said I, ‘I clearly perceive—and
indeed I know, to boot—that your son loves my ward. I am further
very sure that my ward loves your son, but will sacrifice her love to
a sense of duty and affection, and will sacrifice it so completely,
so entirely, so religiously, that you should never suspect it though
you watched her night and day.’ Then I told her all our
story—ours—yours and mine. ‘Now, madam,’ said I, ‘come you, knowing
this, and live with us. Come you, and see my child from hour to hour;
set what you see against her pedigree, which is this, and this’—for
I scorned to mince it—‘and tell me what is the true legitimacy when
you shall have quite made up your mind on that subject.’ Why, honour
to her old Welsh blood, my dear,” cried my guardian with enthusiasm,
“I believe the heart it animates beats no less warmly, no less
admiringly, no less lovingly, towards Dame Durden than my own!”
c64:p35.summary: Jarndyce explains how he told Mrs. Woodcourt of Esther and Woodcourt's love, challenged her prejudices about pedigree, and ultimately convinced her to see Esther's true worth and character.

Come you, and see my child from hour to hour; set what you see against her pedigree, which is this, and this'—for I scorned to mince it—'and tell me what is the true legitimacy when you shall have quite made up your mind on that subject.'
